name: Queen Victoria
role: Queen of the United Kingdom (1837-1901) and Empress of India (1876-1901)
summary: A constitutional monarch who, despite the narrowing of royal power, expressed strong private views: she backed the empire, favoured Disraeli and Salisbury over Gladstone, welcomed the defeat of Irish Home Rule, and opposed votes for women. She supported the 1858 proclamation of religious toleration in India and the 1867 Reform Act, and took some interest in the welfare of the poor.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Reigned as hereditary monarch for 63 years and presided over Jubilee celebrations of the monarchy and empire; no recorded doubt about the institution's legitimacy.

right-to-secede.rationale: In May 1886 she told Gladstone that his Irish measures endangered the Empire, whose union she saw 'in danger of disintegration', and that her silence did not imply approval.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Endorsed Disraeli's expansionist policy including the Zulu and Afghan wars and took the title Empress of India; yet said it was not her custom to annex countries unless obliged and forced.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In August 1858 she asked that the Proclamation to India breathe generosity and religious feeling and point out the privileges the Indians would receive in being placed on an equality with the subjects of the British Crown.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: In January 1874 she wrote to Archbishop Tait that the defiance of the Ritualist clergy was so great that something must be done, wanted laymen mixed with the bishops and an alteration of the Rubric, and backed the Public Worship Regulation Bill passed by Parliament.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Through a 1875 letter sent on her behalf to the Research Defence Society she expressed concern and dismay at vivisection.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Favoured a Royal Commission on housing for the poor and supported charities in education and health.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Succeeded her uncle by hereditary right, took a keen interest in the line of succession as a girl, and her descendants succeeded her.

women-suffrage.rationale: Wrote in 1870 that she was anxious to enlist everyone able to speak or write to check 'this mad, wicked folly of Women's Rights'; Wikipedia records she opposed votes for women.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: In 1886 she objected that Gladstone's plan rested on 'a partially independent Irish authority' and told him she could not support Irish self-government, which she thought endangered the union.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: The Prince Consort's memorandum records that in 1851 the Queen refused Lord Stanley a positive promise of dissolution in advance while promising to discuss it fairly, treating the prerogative as hers to exercise on the occasion.

notes: Most statements are anachronistic or undocumented for her and are left null. Quotations are as reproduced on secondary pages, with some variation in wording. A Rothschild-peerage remark attributed to her was not used because its only source is unreliable. She disliked Gladstone and was privately partisan, so 'nonpartisan-head-of-state' was left null. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by kind; the five Gutenberg texts by her are read by theme and cited or declined; free-trade, which rested only on Wikipedia, is nulled; one new answer from the Prince Consort's 1851 memorandum on dissolution. Her letters are mostly correspondence about ministers, foreign dynasties and the household and rarely state positions on the test's statements.
